node.title: Evolution: Origin of life – Miller’s experiment; Concepts of evolution (Darwin's

questions.stem: Charles Darwin made his five-year voyage around the world aboard the ship
questions.explanation: Darwin travelled on HMS Beagle for about five years and observed the diversity of life, especially on the Galapagos Islands. These observations, together with his reading of Malthus, led him to propose natural selection.

optionRationale.1: HMS Challenger was a later scientific expedition ship, not Darwin's ship.
optionRationale.3: Mayflower carried the Pilgrims to America.

questions.stem: The evolution of many marsupials in Australia from an ancestral stock within the same island continent is an example of
questions.explanation: When different forms evolve from a common ancestor in one geographical area, each adapting to a different habitat or feeding niche, the process is called adaptive radiation. Australian marsupials are a standard example of it.

optionRationale.1: Convergent evolution refers to unrelated groups becoming similar.
optionRationale.2: Genetic drift is a chance change in allele frequencies.
optionRationale.4: Industrial melanism is an example of natural selection in moths.

questions.stem: The theory of the inheritance of acquired characters through use and disuse of organs was proposed by
questions.explanation: Lamarck proposed that organs used more become better developed, and that such acquired changes are passed on to offspring. The example of the giraffe's long neck is often cited. Darwin proposed natural selection instead.

optionRationale.3: Hugo de Vries proposed mutation as the basis of evolution.
optionRationale.4: Haeckel proposed the biogenetic law about embryos.

questions.stem: In Miller's experiment the mixture of gases in the closed flask was subjected to an electric discharge, and the temperature of the flask was kept at about
questions.explanation: In 1953 S. L. Miller passed an electric discharge through a mixture of methane, hydrogen, ammonia and water vapour at 800 °C. After some time amino acids were formed, supporting chemical evolution.

optionRationale.1: 80 °C is too low for this simulation.
optionRationale.2: 8 °C is not the temperature of the experiment.
optionRationale.3: 1800 °C is too high; the textbook value is 800 °C.

questions.stem: The animals believed to have evolved into the first amphibians were the
options: lobefins, fish with stout and strong fins
questions.explanation: Lobe-finned fishes had strong fins with which they could move on land and go back to water. They gave rise to the first amphibians, the first land vertebrates. The coelacanth caught in 1938 is a living example.

optionRationale.1: Jawless fishes were earlier and had no such limbs.
optionRationale.2: Sharks are cartilaginous fishes, not the ancestors of amphibians.

questions.stem: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium the frequency of allele A is 0.7. The frequency of heterozygous Aa individuals is
questions.explanation: If p = 0.7 then q = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3, because the two allele frequencies add up to one. The heterozygote frequency is 2pq, which is 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42.

optionRationale.1: 0.21 is pq and misses the factor 2.
optionRationale.3: 0.49 is p squared, the frequency of AA.
optionRationale.4: 0.09 is q squared, the frequency of aa.

questions.stem: A forest fire kills most of a population at random, and the few survivors have allele frequencies different from the original population. This is an example of the
options: bottleneck effect, a form of genetic drift
questions.explanation: A sudden reduction in population size by chance leaves survivors that need not represent the original gene pool. The resulting random change in allele frequency is genetic drift, here called the bottleneck effect.

optionRationale.2: Selection acts on fitness differences, but here death was random.
optionRationale.3: Gene flow involves migration of individuals between populations.
optionRationale.4: Stabilising selection favours the mean value and is not random.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 1 in 10000 individuals is affected by a recessive disorder. The frequency of carriers is approximately
questions.explanation: The affected frequency is q squared = 0.0001, so q = 0.01 and p = 0.99. The carrier frequency 2pq is 2 × 0.99 × 0.01, which is about 0.02, or 2 in 100.

optionRationale.1: 0.0001 is the frequency of affected individuals, q squared.
optionRationale.2: 0.01 is q, the allele frequency, not the carrier frequency.

questions.stem: Which of the following arranges the hominids in increasing order of brain capacity?
options: Homo erectus, Homo habilis, Neanderthal man
Neanderthal man, Homo erectus, Homo habilis
Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthal man
Homo habilis, Neanderthal man, Homo erectus
questions.explanation: Homo habilis had a brain capacity of about 650 to 800 cc, Homo erectus about 900 cc, and the Neanderthal man about 1400 cc. So the correct increasing order is habilis, erectus, Neanderthal.

optionRationale.1: Homo habilis had a smaller brain than Homo erectus.
optionRationale.4: Homo erectus had a smaller brain than the Neanderthal man.

questions.stem: Match the example in List-I with the concept in List-II.
questions.explanation: Thorns and tendrils have a common origin but different functions, so they are homologous. Octopus and mammalian eyes have similar functions but different origins, so they are analogous. Marsupials show adaptive radiation and dark moths show natural selection.

optionRationale.2: This pairs 'Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita' with 'Analogous structures showing convergent evolution', which describes 'Eyes of octopus and of mammals'.
optionRationale.3: This pairs 'Australian marsupials' with 'Natural selection', which describes 'Dark moths in polluted areas'.
optionRationale.4: This pairs 'Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita' with 'Adaptive radiation', which describes 'Australian marsupials'.

left: A. Thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita
B. Eyes of octopus and of mammals
D. Dark moths in polluted areas
right: I. Homologous structures showing divergent evolution
II. Analogous structures showing convergent evolution

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): According to Hugo de Vries, mutations are random and directionless.
Reason (R): Branching descent and natural selection are the two key concepts of Darwin's theory.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: De Vries proposed that mutations are random and directionless, in contrast with the small, directional variations of Darwin. Darwin's theory rests on branching descent and natural selection. Both are true, but R does not explain A.

optionRationale.1: R does not explain why mutations are random.
optionRationale.4: A is true and R is true.

questions.objective: Contrast mutation theory with Darwin's views

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The flippers of a whale and the fins of a fish are homologous structures.
Reason (R): Both are used for swimming in water.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Homology refers to similar origin, not similar function. The whale's flipper is a modified mammalian forelimb, while a fish fin has a different origin, so they are analogous and A is false. R is true because both are used for swimming.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so both cannot be true.
optionRationale.2: A is false, so both cannot be true.
optionRationale.3: R is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.stem: Match the factor in List-I with its description in List-II.
questions.explanation: Gene migration is movement of individuals, which exchanges alleles between populations. Genetic drift is a chance change in allele frequencies. Mutation creates new alleles, and natural selection favours those with higher reproductive success.

optionRationale.1: This pairs 'Gene migration' with 'Random change in allele frequency, strongest in small populations', which describes 'Genetic drift'.
optionRationale.2: This pairs 'Mutation' with 'Differential reproductive success of individuals', which describes 'Natural selection'.
optionRationale.3: This pairs 'Gene migration' with 'Sudden heritable change in DNA creating new alleles', which describes 'Mutation'.

questions.objective: Match factors that disturb the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

right: I. Sudden heritable change in DNA creating new alleles
II. Movement of individuals into or out of a population
III. Differential reproductive success of individuals
IV. Random change in allele frequency, strongest in small populations

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the origin of life.
A. Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first life originated from pre-existing non-living organic molecules.
B. The age of the earth is about 4.5 billion years.
C. Louis Pasteur supported the theory of spontaneous generation.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Oparin and Haldane proposed chemical evolution of life from non-living molecules, and the earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation by showing that life comes only from pre-existing life, so C is wrong.

optionRationale.2: C is wrong, since Pasteur rejected spontaneous generation.
optionRationale.3: C is wrong and A is correct.
optionRationale.4: C is wrong, so not all three are correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the origin of life

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
A. Allele frequencies remain constant if the population is large, mates randomly and has no migration, mutation or selection.
B. The equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 gives the genotype frequencies.
C. The sum of p and q for two alleles of a gene equals 2.
D. A change in allele frequency is interpreted as evolution.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium holds when no evolutionary forces act, genotype frequencies follow p² + 2pq + q² = 1, and any change in allele frequency means evolution. For two alleles p + q = 1, so C is wrong.

optionRationale.1: D is also correct, so this option is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: C is wrong, and A is correct.
optionRationale.4: C is wrong, so not all four are correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the Hardy-Weinberg principle
